blocks.text: 1. Collections

blocks.alt: Data type A goes into collection A while data type B goes into collection B

blocks.text: Indexing covered organizing vectors for fast search within a single index. Collections cover how a vector database organizes vectors into separate logical groups, moving from a single index to organizing many of them.
It groups related vectors together so searches can stay scoped to the right subset.
2. One Big Pile Versus Separate Groups
Storing every vector in one undivided pile forces every query to search across unrelated content too.
Collections let a pipeline group vectors that belong together.
3. What Defines A Collection Boundary

blocks.alt: Same embedding model and same use case both define collection boundaries

blocks.text: A collection boundary often follows a natural split, like separate products, tenants, or document types.
Each collection gets its own dedicated index.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Common collection boundary","Example"],"rows":[["By tenant","Each customer's data lives in its own collection"],["By content type","Documentation, support tickets, and product data in separate collections"]]}

blocks.text: 4. A Query Searches One Collection At A Time

blocks.alt: A query searches one collection to produce results

blocks.text: A typical search targets one specific collection rather than the entire database.
This narrows the search scope before similarity comparison ever even begins.
5. Multi Tenant Isolation

blocks.alt: Tenant A collection is isolated from tenant B collection

blocks.text: A multi tenant application often gives each customer their own separate collection.
This guarantees one tenant's search never accidentally surfaces another tenant's data.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Mixing multiple tenants into one shared collection without careful filtering creates a real risk that one customer's search could accidentally return another customer's private data if that filtering logic ever has a bug.

blocks.text: 6. Collections Versus Metadata Filtering

blocks.alt: Collections form a hard boundary while metadata filtering forms a soft boundary

blocks.text: As with metadata filtering, covered as the next topic in this module, a collection is a hard, structural boundary.
Metadata filtering instead applies a softer, more flexible boundary within a single collection.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Boundary type","Flexibility"],"rows":[["Collection","Hard, structural separation, its own index"],["Metadata filtering, covered next in this module","Soft, flexible filtering within one shared collection"]]}

blocks.text: 7. Collection Specific Configuration

blocks.alt: A collection has its own index settings

blocks.text: Different collections can use different embedding models or different index settings entirely.
As with choosing a dimension count in Embedding Dimensions, each collection can be tuned independently for its own content.
8. The Overhead Of Many Collections
An extremely large number of tiny collections adds real management overhead.
Each collection carries its own index and configuration to maintain.
9. Recognizing When Separate Collections Make Sense

blocks.alt: Distinct data types or tenants point toward using separate collections

blocks.text: Multi tenant systems and distinct content types benefit from separate collections.
One small, homogeneous content set can live comfortably in a single collection.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Storing all data in one giant collection when clear natural boundaries like tenants exist.
Confusing a collection boundary with metadata filtering, when the two serve different purposes.
Creating an excessive number of tiny collections, adding unnecessary management overhead.
Forgetting that each collection can be independently configured for its own specific content.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Collections group related vectors together so searches stay scoped to the right subset.
Storing everything in one pile forces every query to search across unrelated content too.
A collection boundary often follows a natural split, like tenants or content types.
A typical search targets one specific collection, narrowing scope before comparison begins.
Multi tenant applications often use separate collections to guarantee data isolation.
A collection is a hard, structural boundary; metadata filtering is a softer, flexible one.
Different collections can use different embedding models or index settings independently.
An excessive number of tiny collections adds real index and configuration management overhead.
